summary: Defines a certificate extension for the self-signed certificate of a root certification authority. The extension carries a hash that unambiguously identifies the next public key that will replace the current root key at some future point, which helps with planned root key transitions.

eli5.summary: A king can leave a sealed note saying who the next king will be, so people know to trust the right one later. This is a note like that for certificate authorities.

questions: how to announce next root certificate
subtitle: Announcing the next root CA key so relying parties can smoothly transition

tldr.problem: When a root certificate authority needs to replace its key, relying parties (systems that trust the CA) must somehow know that the new certificate is legitimate and should replace the old one. Without this mechanism, the transition is risky and requires coordination.
tldr.mechanism: The Hash Of Root Key extension in a root certificate contains a hash of the next-generation public key, allowing any relying party to recognize and validate the successor certificate when it is released, by verifying the certificate signature and checking that its public key hash matches.
tldr.outcome: Root CA key transitions can be orderly and decentralized without requiring all relying parties to update at the same time or requiring a coordination mechanism.

today: RFC 8649 is an Informational specification and remains the definitive guidance for planning root CA key transitions. It has not been obsoleted. Some PKI systems (such as CTIA wireless PKI) have adopted this extension, and it is recommended for any root CA that needs to manage planned key rollover.

sections.title: Root Certificate Key Transitions
sections.content:
The Hash Of Root Key is an optional X.509 version 3 certificate extension carried in the self-signed certificate of a root certification authority (CA). It facilitates the orderly transition from one Root CA public key to the next.

The extension contains a hash value of the next-generation public key, which acts as a commitment. Before the current root certificate expires, when the time comes to deploy a new root certificate with a different key, any relying party can verify that the new certificate's public key matches the hash from the previous one. This unambiguous link between the current root and its successor eliminates the risk that an attacker or misconfiguration causes relying parties to install the wrong certificate.
sections.eli5: Before a king retires, he seals a letter with the fingerprint of his successor. When the successor arrives, people check the fingerprint, see it matches, and safely accept the new king.

sections.title: How the Transition Works
sections.content:
Before initial deployment, the root CA generates an initial key pair (R1), a second-generation key pair (R2), and computes a hash of R2 called H2. The initial self-signed certificate for R1 is created with the HashOfRootKey extension containing H2.

Later, when it is time to replace R1, the root CA generates a third-generation key pair (R3), computes its hash H3, and creates a self-signed certificate for R2 that includes H3. This is an iterative process: each certificate points to its successor.

When a relying party receives a potential next-generation certificate, it verifies the certificate signature (ensuring the key owner created it) and checks that the hash of the DER-encoded public key matches the value in the current certificate's HashOfRootKey extension. If both checks succeed, the certificate is valid and can be added to the trust anchor store.
sections.eli5: Step 1: First leader signs a letter saying "Next, trust this fingerprint." Step 2: New leader arrives and we check their fingerprint against the letter. Step 3: If it matches, we trust them. Step 4: New leader signs a letter saying who comes after them, and repeat.

sections.title: The Extension Structure
sections.content:
The HashOfRootKey extension is defined as an ASN.1 SEQUENCE containing two fields: hashAlg (the hash algorithm used, such as SHA-256) and hashValue (the hash value as an octet string). The extension is not critical, meaning that systems which do not understand it can still process the certificate.

The hash value is computed from the DER-encoded SubjectPublicKeyInfo (the public key structure as it appears in the X.509 certificate), not just the key bits. This ensures that the complete key structure, including its algorithm identifiers and parameters, is covered by the hash. The Object Identifier for this extension is 1.3.6.1.4.1.51483.2.1.
sections.eli5: The extension is like a sealed envelope that says "I used SHA-256 to fingerprint the next key, and here is the fingerprint.� It is not required to understand this, so old systems still work.

sections.title: Security and Operational Safeguards
sections.content:
The root CA must use a cryptographically strong hash function resistant to preimage attacks (such as SHA-256). A preimage attack would allow an attacker to find a different key that produces the same hash, which could trick relying parties into trusting an unauthorized key.

The root CA must securely back up the next-generation key pair before publishing the hash. If the hardware security module holding the key fails, the root CA becomes committed to a key pair that is no longer available, and must deploy an entirely new certificate and key, losing the benefits of the extension.

When the transition occurs, ICANN and enterprise PKI guidelines recommend publishing both the oldWithNew certificate (signed by the old key, valid for all certificates issued under the old key) and the newWithOld certificate (signed by the new key, demonstrating the new key is operational) before removing the old certificate from trust stores. This ensures that relying parties validating certificates issued under both keys do not experience failures during the transition window.
sections.eli5: The fingerprint must be very hard to fake. The root CA must keep the next key safe or it will be stuck. And the transition should be gradual, with both the old and new leaders signing documents for a while so no one is left holding invalid credentials.

sections.title: Deployment and Adoption
sections.content:
The extension is optional and backward compatible. A root CA can include it or omit it. In environments with a certificate directory (such as enterprise PKIs), the CA can publish intermediate certificates and certificates of both generations before making the transition. In environments without such infrastructure (such as the Web PKI), the root CA uses the Subject Information Access extension to point to a URL where relying parties can fetch both the old and new certificates.

Relying parties without knowledge of the HashOfRootKey extension will simply continue using the old root certificate until it expires. This allows a gradual, non-coordinated migration where different systems can adopt the new certificate at different times.
sections.eli5: Systems that know about this feature can upgrade to the new root immediately when they see the fingerprint match. Systems that do not know about it will use the old root until it stops working, and then upgrade. No one has to coordinate.

events.label: Initial deployment: R1 key with hash of R2
Transition: R2 key with hash of R3
Next transition: R3 key with hash of R4
